title: Magnetic Induction
short_intro: Magnetic induction refers to the production of an electromotive force (EMF) or current in a conductor when it is exposed to a changing magnetic field or when relative motion exists between the conductor and the magnetic field. It is governed fundamentally by Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction and Lenz's law.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction, Lenz's law, magnitude and direction of induced EMF, self-induction, mutual induction, and simple numericals on magnetic flux linked with coils.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Differential and integral forms of Maxwell's equations relating to electromagnetic induction, vector potential, eddy currents, betatron principle, and complex mutual inductance problems in coupled circuits.

prerequisites: Biot-Savart Law and Ampere's Circuital Law
Magnetic flux and its spatial variation
Basic vector calculus and divergence/curl operations (for PGT)

concept_notes.heading: Faraday's Laws of Electromagnetic Induction
bullets: First Law: Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a closed circuit changes, an induced electromotive force (EMF) is set up in the circuit.
Second Law: The magnitude of the induced EMF is directly proportional to the time rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit.
Mathematical expression: e = -dPhi/dt for a single turn, and e = -N(dPhi/dt) for a coil of N turns.

concept_notes.heading: Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
bullets: Lenz's Law states that the polarity of the induced EMF is such that it tends to oppose the very cause (change in magnetic flux) that produces it.
The negative sign in Faraday's law equation explicitly incorporates Lenz's law.
Lenz's law is a direct consequence of the law of conservation of energy; mechanical work done in moving a conductor through a magnetic field transforms into electrical energy.

concept_notes.heading: Self-Induction and Self-Inductance
bullets: Self-induction is the property of a single coil by virtue of which it opposes any change in the strength of current flowing through it by inducing an opposing EMF.
The magnetic flux linked with the coil is directly proportional to the current flowing through it: Phi = L * I.
Self-inductance (L) depends on the geometry of the coil, number of turns, and the permeability of the core medium, with SI unit Henry (H).

concept_notes.heading: Mutual Induction and Mutual Inductance
bullets: Mutual induction is the phenomenon where a changing current in one coil induces an EMF in a neighboring secondary coil.
The flux linked with the secondary coil is proportional to the current in the primary coil: Phi_2 = M * I_1.
Mutual inductance (M) depends on the separation, relative orientation, and magnetic coupling between the two coils.

derivations.title: Self-Inductance of a Long Solenoid
derivations.conditions: Long air-cored solenoid of length l, cross-sectional area A, and total turns N.
steps: Write the magnetic field inside the long solenoid: B = mu_0 * n * I, where n = N / l is the number of turns per unit length.
Calculate the magnetic flux linked with a single turn: Phi_{single} = B * A = mu_0 * (N/l) * I * A.
Calculate the total magnetic flux linked with all N turns: Phi_{total} = N * Phi_{single} = mu_0 * (N^2 / l) * A * I.
Equate total flux to L * I to find the self-inductance: L * I = mu_0 * (N^2 / l) * A * I.

derivations.title: Induced EMF in a Rod Rotating in a Uniform Magnetic Field
derivations.conditions: A metallic rod of length l rotating with angular velocity omega in a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to the plane of rotation.
steps: Consider an infinitesimal element of the rod of length dr at a distance r from the axis of rotation.
The linear velocity of this element is v = omega * r.
The motional EMF induced across the element dr is de = B * v * dr = B * omega * r * dr.
Integrate the infinitesimal EMF from r = 0 to r = l to find the total induced EMF: e = int_{0}^{l} B omega r , dr.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetic Flux vs. Time Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting magnetic flux (Phi) on the y-axis against time (t) on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The instantaneous slope (negative derivative) at any point on the curve gives the magnitude of the induced EMF at that exact instant.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in conceptual multiple-choice questions to determine times of maximum and zero induced EMF.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Growth of Current in an L-R Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An exponential growth curve of current (I) against time (t) asymptoting to maximum value I_0 = E/R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The time constant (	au = L/R) represents the time required for the current to reach approximately 63.2% of its maximum steady-state value.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested numerically and conceptually for transient behavior in inductive circuits.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Electromagnetic Induction Experiment (Magnet and Coil)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bar magnet moving toward a solenoid connected to a sensitive center-zero galvanometer.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that relative motion generates current; reversing the motion or polarity of the magnet reverses the galvanometer deflection direction.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Asked in descriptive or foundational principle questions regarding Faraday and Lenz laws.

solved_numericals.question: A coil of 500 turns has a magnetic flux of 0.02 Wb linked with it. If the flux is reduced to zero in 0.1 seconds, find the induced EMF in the coil.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: N = 500, initial flux Phi_1 = 0.02 Wb, final flux Phi_2 = 0, time interval Delta t = 0.1 s.
Calculate change in flux: Delta Phi = Phi_2 - Phi_1 = 0 - 0.02 = -0.02 Wb.
Apply Faraday's law: e = -N * (Delta Phi / Delta t) = -500 * (-0.02 / 0.1).

solved_numericals.question: The self-inductance of a coil is 5 H. If a current of 2 A is reversed to 2 A in 0.05 seconds, calculate the average induced EMF.
solution_steps: Identify parameters: L = 5 H, initial current I_1 = 2 A, final current I_2 = -2 A, Delta t = 0.05 s.
Calculate change in current: Delta I = I_2 - I_1 = -2 - 2 = -4 A.
Apply induced EMF formula for inductance: e = -L * (Delta I / Delta t).

solved_numericals.question: Two coaxial solenoids each of length 1 m have inner radius 2 cm and outer radius 3 cm. The inner solenoid has 1000 turns and the outer solenoid has 1500 turns. Find the mutual inductance between them.
solution_steps: Identify overlapping cross-sectional area common to both solenoids, determined by the inner radius r = 0.02 m: A = pi * r^2 = pi * (0.02)^2 = 4pi * 10^{-4} m^2.
Write the formula for mutual inductance of coaxial solenoids: M = mu_0 * (N_1 * N_2 / l) * A.
Substitute the given values: mu_0 = 4pi * 10^{-7}, N_1 = 1000, N_2 = 1500, l = 1 m, A = 4pi * 10^{-4} m^2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Solenoid formulas assume an infinitely long solenoid where edge effects and magnetic flux leakage at the ends are negligible.
Uniformity of magnetic field is assumed over the entire cross-sectional area of the loop unless spatial integration is explicitly performed.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An EMF is induced only when the magnetic field B itself changes.
common_misconceptions.correct: An EMF is induced whenever the total magnetic flux (Phi = B * A * cos	heta) changes, which can happen by changing B, area A, or angle 	heta.
common_misconceptions.why: Students often confuse magnetic field strength with magnetic flux linkage.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Lenz's law implies that the induced EMF cancels out the applied change completely.
common_misconceptions.correct: Lenz's law opposes the change, but it cannot prevent the change from happening; otherwise, continuous induction would violate energy conservation.
common_misconceptions.why: Misinterpretation of the word 'opposition' leads to the belief that net flux cannot change.

quick_revision: Induced EMF depends strictly on the rate of change of magnetic flux, not on the total flux value itself.
